payload.instructions: Return only the requested structured result. Classify consensus distance without deciding the full chapter's persuasiveness.
payload.input:
You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Stranger

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, the 'stranger' (Hebrew ger, sojourner; Greek xenos) primarily symbolizes the vulnerable outsider in whom God—and specifically Christ—is encountered, so that hospitality to the stranger is treated as a test and expression of covenant faithfulness and love of God. The stranger stands for the marginalized person whom God commands his people to welcome, protect, and love, grounded in Israel's own memory of being strangers in Egypt and culminating in Jesus' identification of himself with the stranger.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Matthew 25:35, 38, 43-44 ('I was a stranger and you welcomed me')",
    "Leviticus 19:33-34 ('love the stranger as yourself, for you were strangers in Egypt')",
    "Exodus 22:21 and 23:9 (do not wrong or oppress a stranger)",
    "Deuteronomy 10:18-19 (God loves the stranger; you shall love the stranger)",
    "Hebrews 13:2 (entertaining strangers, some have entertained angels unawares)",
    "Genesis 18:1-8 (Abraham's hospitality to three strangers)",
    "Luke 24:13-35 (the risen Christ unrecognized as a stranger on the Emmaus road)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Believers themselves as 'strangers and pilgrims/exiles' on earth—a symbol of the Christian's true citizenship in heaven and detachment from the present world. This is a very widespread second stream of interpretation, prominent in Puritan, pietist, and pilgrimage theology.",
      "basis": [
        "Hebrews 11:13 ('strangers and pilgrims on the earth')",
        "1 Peter 1:1 and 2:11 ('sojourners and exiles')",
        "Genesis 23:4 and Psalm 39:12 ('I am a stranger with thee, a sojourner')",
        "Philippians 3:20 (citizenship in heaven)",
        "1 Chronicles 29:15"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The stranger as a symbol of alienation from God and the covenant—those 'strangers to the covenants of promise' who are brought near in Christ; welcome of the outsider then symbolizes Gentile inclusion in the people of God.",
      "basis": [
        "Ephesians 2:12, 19 ('no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens')",
        "Isaiah 56:3-7 (the foreigner joined to the LORD)",
        "Colossians 1:21"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The stranger as a negative figure: the false shepherd or false teacher whose voice the sheep do not follow, or the 'strange woman' of Proverbs symbolizing temptation, folly, or apostasy.",
      "basis": [
        "John 10:5 ('a stranger will they not follow... they know not the voice of strangers')",
        "Proverbs 2:16; 5:3-20; 7:5 (the 'strange woman')"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Christ himself as the divine Stranger—unrecognized, rejected, appearing incognito among his own—a devotional and literary reading built on the Emmaus narrative, Matthew 25, and John 1.",
      "basis": [
        "Luke 24:13-35",
        "John 1:10-11 ('the world knew him not; his own received him not')",
        "Matthew 25:35"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "medium",
  "notes": "'Stranger' carries a recognizable but two-sided consensus rather than a single fixed symbol: (1) the outsider to be welcomed, in whom Christ is met (hospitality/love of neighbor), and (2) the believer's own status as a sojourner whose home is heaven. Both are broadly attested across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant teaching; the hospitality/Matthew 25 reading is the most frequently cited in modern preaching and social teaching, while the pilgrim reading dominates in devotional and eschatological contexts. Which is 'primary' depends on tradition and era, so confidence is rated medium. Negative uses (John 10:5; the strange woman of Proverbs) are real but clearly secondary in the interpretive literature."
}

RESPONSE B
{
  "primary_meaning": "Believers living as temporary residents or pilgrims in the earthly world, signifying that their ultimate citizenship, allegiance, and home belong to the Kingdom of Heaven.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Hebrews 11:13",
    "1 Peter 1:1",
    "1 Peter 2:11",
    "Philippians 3:20"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "The vulnerable, marginalized person, or Christ himself in disguise, to whom believers are commanded to show hospitality and love.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:35",
        "Hebrews 13:2",
        "Deuteronomy 10:19"
      ],
      "prominence": "dominant"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Gentiles or unbelievers who were formerly alienated from God's covenants of promise, but are now brought near through Christ.",
      "basis": [
        "Ephesians 2:12",
        "Ephesians 2:19"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "The symbolism of the stranger or sojourner is well-established in two main streams of Christian thought: the believer's existential alienation from the fallen world (pilgrim theology) and the ethical mandate of hospitality where the stranger represents the presence of Christ."
}

RESPONSE C
{
  "primary_meaning": "An outsider or alien—especially someone separated from God’s covenant people, but capable of being welcomed and incorporated into the community. In many passages “stranger” is first a literal social category rather than a fixed symbol; Christian interpretation often extends it to spiritual alienation and reconciliation.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Ephesians 2:12, 19 — Gentiles were “strangers to the covenants of promise” but become members of God’s household.",
    "Leviticus 19:33–34 — Israel must love the stranger residing among them as themselves.",
    "Deuteronomy 10:18–19 — God loves the stranger, and Israel is commanded to do likewise.",
    "Isaiah 56:3–8 — foreigners who join themselves to the Lord are welcomed among God’s people.",
    "Colossians 1:21–22 — alienation from God followed by reconciliation, although many translations do not use “stranger.”"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "The believer as a pilgrim or temporary resident in the present world, whose true homeland is heavenly.",
      "basis": [
        "Hebrews 11:13–16 — the faithful confess that they are strangers and pilgrims on earth and seek a heavenly country.",
        "1 Peter 2:11 — Christians are addressed as strangers, exiles, or sojourners.",
        "Philippians 3:20 — believers’ citizenship is in heaven."
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The vulnerable outsider in whom Christ is encountered and to whom hospitality and mercy must be shown.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:35, 38, 43–45 — welcoming the stranger is treated as welcoming Christ.",
        "Hebrews 13:2 — hospitality to strangers may amount to entertaining angels.",
        "Luke 10:25–37 — the outsider becomes the exemplary neighbor, though the word “stranger” is not the central term."
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A person whose voice or teaching does not belong to Christ, and whom Christ’s sheep therefore refuse to follow.",
      "basis": [
        "John 10:5 — the sheep flee from a stranger because they do not recognize the stranger’s voice.",
        "John 10:1–10 — the surrounding shepherd imagery associates unauthorized figures with danger to the flock."
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Christ himself as unrecognized, rejected, or apparently foreign to those he visits.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:35–40 — Christ identifies himself with the stranger who is welcomed.",
        "Luke 24:18 — the risen Jesus is initially treated as a stranger by the disciples on the Emmaus road.",
        "John 1:10–11 — Christ comes to his own but is not received, though “stranger” is not explicitly used."
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is no single settled biblical symbolism for “stranger.” The term often denotes an actual foreigner, resident alien, guest, or unknown person. Its meaning also varies with the underlying Hebrew and Greek terms, including ger (resident alien/sojourner), nokri (foreigner), xenos (stranger/foreigner), and paroikos (sojourner). The outsider or alien is the broadest recurring theological association, while the pilgrim-believer and Christ-in-the-stranger readings are also well established."
}

RESPONSE D
{
  "primary_meaning": "The Christian believer (or people of God) as a temporary sojourner, pilgrim, or exile on earth whose true citizenship and home are in heaven",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Hebrews 11:13",
    "1 Peter 2:11",
    "Psalm 39:12",
    "Psalm 119:19",
    "Hebrews 13:14",
    "Philippians 3:20"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "The foreigner/resident alien (ger/xenos) who must receive justice, protection, and hospitality as a reflection of God's character and Israel's own experience as strangers in Egypt",
      "basis": [
        "Leviticus 19:33-34",
        "Deuteronomy 10:18-19",
        "Exodus 22:21",
        "Exodus 23:9",
        "Matthew 25:35"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Christ himself present in and identified with the needy outsider or guest",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:35-40"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The people of God (Israel or the church) living in diaspora or exile status among the nations",
      "basis": [
        "1 Peter 1:1",
        "Genesis 23:4",
        "Jeremiah 29",
        "Psalm 137"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "The term functions both ethically (OT law of the ger) and spiritually (NT pilgrim identity); the pilgrim/exile motif is the most frequent traditional symbolic application in Christian teaching and spirituality, yet ethical hospitality readings remain equally widespread, especially in modern interpretation. No single exclusive symbolic consensus exists."
}

BOOK ENTRY
A non-citizen of God's commonwealth — one outside the covenant, drawn in, or, once in, made a stranger to the world.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
(none)

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Eph 2:12, 19) · see Orphans, Widows & the Fatherless, ch. 14

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Ephesians 2:12 — That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:
Ephesians 2:19 — Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
